data.name: Bubbles
data.title: A game can work and still be waiting to feel finished.
data.summary: Bubbles is a polished arcade game with a serious deterministic core. Its remaining work is concentrated in the connected product experience, broad browser qualification and owner acceptance.
data.why: The interesting question has changed. Bubbles no longer needs to prove that a game exists; it needs to prove that the whole product holds together across screens, states and actual play.
data.teaches: Closing an issue is a record of work. It is not proof that the product has finished the job.

data.name: Fighter
data.title: The game is real. The quality bar is deliberately unreasonable.
data.summary: Fighter includes Story, Tournament, Battle, Arcade, Survival, Daily Challenges and progression. The remaining work is a whole-game review against the A+ bar.
data.why: A large feature set can hide weak moments. Fighter is a proving ground for the difference between a technically complete game and one that feels authored from first run through the result.
data.teaches: Passing geometry checks does not settle visual hierarchy, role, motion or whether a screen feels right in context.

data.name: MAX
data.title: The software cannot prove that a person can find the real walker.
data.summary: MAX is an assistive-technology project with a substantial software platform: PWA, pairing, gateway, offline behaviour, remote FIND and STOP, privacy and device control.
data.why: The product crosses a physical boundary. Simulation and a green software suite cannot prove that a real walker, microphone, speaker and lights work for a person in their environment.
data.teaches: Software proof and physical proof are different kinds of evidence.

data.name: Pirates
data.title: Reconstruct the original game before asking the agents to invent another one.
data.summary: Pirates is rebuilding Master of the Secret Sea from original source evidence. The work is deliberately parity-first.
data.why: Generative systems are good at filling gaps. In a reconstruction, that instinct can quietly turn an unknown into a confident invention. The project has to know what the source proves and what it does not.
data.teaches: Sometimes the most intelligent agent action is to stop at the edge of the evidence.

data.name: LoftwahFM
data.title: One music catalogue. Independent games. Evidence for each.
data.summary: LoftwahFM owns the music catalogue, radio generation, station programming and shared browser client. Listen to its music stations and first original shows, then follow the separate evidence for game adoption. The broader venue business remains a separate roadmap.
data.why: Games can reuse published music and a compatible client while retaining their own sound, settings, lifecycle and release gates. Music availability does not establish in-game adoption or demand for a venue product.
data.teaches: A shared capability earns its name through compatible releases and real consumers. Published upstream code and verified game use are different evidence.

data.name: Asset Hunter
data.discipline: Discovery engine · creative and technical reference
data.title: A discovery engine has to be willing to report that nobody is using it.
data.summary: Asset Hunter is a discovery engine, not a catalogue. A separate crawl-and-inspect engine reads licences from the bytes it downloads, groups material into distinct possibilities across games, interface, branding, motion, audio, 3D, shaders, code and architecture, and publishes them into a public EmDash site on Cloudflare through a contract rather than by touching the CMS directly. Each possibility carries representative examples, build notes, a prompt scaffold and a per-example rights statement. The repository is public, the site is public, and the product verifies its own deployment: it names the commit it was built from, and its restore drill reports honestly when the data it protects is empty.
data.why: It keeps two things apart that are easy to conflate. Learning that a treatment exists is not permission to copy the asset that demonstrated it, so rights are recorded per example and reference-only material is never presented as cleared. It keeps a third apart: an engine that can find, classify and publish is implementation, and shipping it is release, and neither one is demand. Its own backup records that nobody has yet rated, reported, disputed or objected to anything it found.
data.teaches: A public product can publish its own evidence and its own negative evidence. This one names the exact commit it serves, and its restore drill exits non-zero because the tables that would hold a stranger's judgement have never held a row.

data.title: Eight projects. Eight different finish lines.
data.deck: A fresh review of the factory's eight projects separates what each can do from the evidence and decisions still needed.
data.source_reference: Shareable factory portfolio report reviewed 1 October 2026. Edited, public-safe summaries; private issue, pull request and conversation bodies are not reproduced.
data.lead: The most useful result was not a ranking. It was a clear boundary between what each project can do and what still needs proof.
data.lesson: A portfolio has no single finish line. Each project's state belongs to its own evidence and review date.

children.text: This review puts eight projects on one dated page without pretending they share one definition of done. Some work is held by product quality, some by release evidence, some by source parity, and some by a real-world hardware trial.
Read each project on its own terms

Every project has its own dossier on this site. Each one states the reviewed state, the next useful proof and the boundary that state does not cross. A strong software result does not certify a finished product, and a past production observation does not establish that today's source is live.
Implementation, qualification, production verification and physical proof remain four separate records. Collapsing them is the most common way a portfolio report overstates a factory.
What the report keeps separate
Four boundaries run through every project in this factory, and each one has cost real work when it was blurred.
Implementation is not qualification. Code that exists and has been reviewed is a different record from code that has passed the checks required to be released.
A production claim belongs to the exact version observed. A deployment receipt names one Worker version and one review date; it does not speak for later source.
Software tests cannot prove how physical hardware behaves for a person in the world. That claim needs a physical trial and a dated observation.
Unknown source behaviour stays unknown until evidence resolves it. A reconstruction that cannot be read is recorded as ambiguous, not guessed.

content.quote: Progress is real when the work moves. Completion is real when the required evidence supports the claim.

children.text: How to read this report

Every project dossier states its own review date and source. Where this report summarises a project, the dossier is the authority; where the two disagree, the dossier and its dated snapshot are what the site publishes.

data.title: I Didn't Mean to Build a Software Factory
data.deck: A practical habit of composing tools grew into a system for directing software agents, checking their work and seeing what survived in the real world.
data.source_reference: Founder-supplied professional retrospective and the shareable factory snapshot reviewed 28 September 2026.
data.lead: The work began with making software. It grew into a system for deciding what the software had actually proved.
data.lesson: The factory exists to make intent, work and evidence legible across products.

children.text: The first part of the story was ordinary web work: joining useful tools together instead of rebuilding each capability. A reverse proxy, a VPS and WordPress plugins formed a practical stack. The skill that lasted was composition: knowing which piece was good at a job and how to make the pieces cooperate.

The tools changed. Plugin-shaped capability gave way to APIs, cloud services, infrastructure, models, skills and agents. Development moved from assembling a website toward operating the platform and its delivery system.
When one pair became a working system

A coding agent first changes how one person writes software. Multiple agents change the shape of the work. Requests need to become bounded tasks; people and agents need clear ownership; competing changes need review; and release evidence must be attached to the exact state being claimed.

The supplied founding account describes agents working across several products for extended stretches. At that point, writing code was no longer the only bottleneck. The operator needed to see which work had started, what had changed, what had survived review and what still needed proof.

content.title: From pair programming to factory
content.note: The operator supplies intent and remains accountable while bounded work moves through agents, review, qualification and production.

children.text: A backlog is useful when it tells the truth

Delegation creates a new coordination problem. The task list has to show what the work means, who can act on it and which evidence closes it. Repository state and review records then provide a durable account that survives a chat ending or an agent stopping.

A green check cannot inherit authority it was never designed to provide. A build can establish that code compiled. Review can challenge a proposed change. Qualification can test a candidate. Only a live observation can support a production claim, and only the owner can decide whether the result meets the intended bar.
The system therefore needs to preserve several kinds of state instead of compressing them into a single percentage or a vague “done.”
Failures become useful when the control changes

The factory’s projects expose different edges of the same problem. In Fighter, geometry checks passed while the interface still missed its visual purpose. Pirates has to account for original source rules before agents invent an expansion. MAX cannot use a browser test as evidence that a person can find the real walker. Bubbles can be functionally mature while browser and owner acceptance remain open.

These are not interchangeable bugs. Each needs its own evidence. The general pattern is to record what was expected, observe what happened, name the class of failure and put a control where it can catch the same mistake again.

content.title: The failure loop
content.note: A lesson only becomes a factory control when it changes how later work is reviewed or qualified.

children.text: Trust is a ladder, not a label

The operating model separates what was observed from what was implemented, merged, qualified, verified in production and accepted by the owner. A project may have strong evidence at one rung and an open question on another.

children.text: Why Woodhouse exists

Once the factory had several active products, a public record became another useful system: a place to see what each project is for, what its reviewed status means and which evidence is still missing. Woodhouse is designed for people and for agents that need a machine-readable account with clear limits.

This first release is a dated, operator-supplied portfolio snapshot. It does not connect to private repositories, stream GitHub activity or publish working conversations. Agent Reception is read-only. Those boundaries keep the public record useful without pretending it is live telemetry.
See how the projects currently stand, or read the factory doctrine that governs their evidence.

data.title: The tests passed. The game still looked wrong.
data.deck: Fighter passed its geometry checks and still fell short of the product bar. The factory had measured whether the interface fitted. It had not measured whether the interface worked as a composition.
data.source_reference: Shareable factory snapshot reviewed 28 September 2026; no private repository or conversation material is reproduced.
data.lead: The interface did what the tests could see. The tests could not see what the player felt.
data.lesson: Geometry is evidence about geometry. Product judgement needs its own review.

children.text: The wrong question was easy to test.
The checks asked whether the interface fit its container and whether its geometry remained inside expected bounds. It did. The result still lacked hierarchy and compositional intent.
That was not a failure of the geometry checks. They answered the question they were built to answer. The mistake was treating their answer as a complete product judgement.

content.title: Initial belief
content.body: Responsive geometry and screenshot checks would prevent the important visual failures.

children.text: What the evidence could not see
A page can avoid clipping and still put the wrong thing first. A screen can be dimensionally correct while the player has to work to understand what matters, what changed or where to go next.

The factory therefore added three human checks: a visual review of the whole experience, a review of complete journeys and a copy check for generic or machine-written language. Reviewers identify the focal point, hierarchy, competing elements, context and quality of the complete experience.

content.quote: Geometry is evidence about geometry. It is not evidence that the product feels finished.

children.text: The lesson travelled

The same distinction later mattered in Bubbles: a technically valid interface was still challenged against its actual product bar. The factory’s lesson was not to discard automation. It was to stop asking one instrument to certify a different kind of quality.
What changed in the factory

Visual review became a named qualification stage. Whole journeys are reviewed with the implementation context in view. Responsive quality is judged at the states and orientations where people use the product. Passing a machine check is reported only as the claim that check supports.

data.title: Prove which build is live, or admit you do not know
data.deck: A public origin could not state which source it was serving. Rather than document that gap, this closes it: the build stamps its own fingerprint, the origin publishes it, and the deploy refuses to finish if the two disagree.
data.source_reference: The Woodhouse repository itself: the build-identity integration, the /build.json route, the shared verifier and the production deploy gate, reviewed 4 October 2026.
data.lead: A deploy receipt records what was intended to ship. For a long time nothing recorded what the public origin was actually serving, so those stayed two different claims.
data.lesson: A deployment that cannot report its own identity cannot be verified as current. Publishing the fingerprint is what turns "deployed" into "serving this exact build".

children.text: This was not a missing feature so much as a missing question. Every repository in this factory writes deploy notes, and several of them record a receipt naming a commit and a release. What none of them could do was ask the live origin what it was serving and get an answer. So a green deploy and a stale production could look identical from the outside, and the difference only surfaced later, as a bug report.

One product in this factory discovered the same gap from the other direction: it found production running behind its own default branch, with several hundred audit findings that were really just staleness. It had no way to name the live commit. That is the failure this work removes.
What the build stamps

A small build step computes a fingerprint over the exact source files that go into a deploy, alongside the commit that working tree sat on and whether that tree was clean. The value is substituted into the bundle at compile time, so nothing extra is written into the source tree and the deployed artefact carries no new file.

Reporting the tree's cleanliness matters more than it looks. A build made from a dirty tree corresponds to no reviewable commit at all, so a receipt naming a commit would be describing something that never existed as a unit.
What the origin refuses to claim

The endpoint does not report a Cloudflare Worker version identifier, because the runtime cannot know it. Only the deploy tool's output reveals it, and that value belongs in the private release receipt where it was observed rather than inferred.

That distinction is the whole point. An endpoint that could only approximate its own identity would eventually be quoted as though it were exact, and a number that is nearly right is worse than one that is honestly absent.
The gate is the useful half
Publishing an identity proves nothing on its own. The control that matters is the comparison.

Both deploy paths now read the live origin after deployment and refuse to continue unless the fingerprint it reports is the one that run just built. Preview is held to the same standard, because a preview that cannot prove its own source cannot support a production acceptance receipt.

The check was written once and shared. Standing alone it answers the question that is otherwise pure guesswork, which is what any given origin is serving right now. That matters most for products this factory does not own, where nobody has local access to compare against.

content.quote: A deployment that cannot report its own identity cannot be verified as current.

children.text: Reuse across the factory

The identity shape is deliberately small and published as a versioned schema, so a single verifier can check any product that adopts it. The products can keep their own judgement about what should ship; only the mechanism for proving what is live is meant to be shared.

This is the intended division: centralise the mechanism, keep the product judgement local. A shared media pipeline, a repository census or a resource lease earns the same treatment, but only once it has been shown to be genuinely the same problem in more than one place.

Adopting it is not retroactive. Nothing here claims another product publishes this yet, and no product is named as compliant. The capability exists, one product uses it, and the rest are free to ignore it until the question comes up.

children.text: Asset Hunter is the ninth project on this site and the first one whose evidence anyone outside the factory can check. Its repository is public, its site publishes the commit it was built from, and its catalogue states its own size. Everything else here is an operator-reviewed summary of work the public cannot see.

The portfolio is reviewed project by project, not all at once, so this record now reports its newest review and says how many projects predate it. The eight launch projects still carry their 28 September 2026 date. Nothing about them was re-reviewed today, and nothing about them was changed.
What a public repository allows Woodhouse to claim

On 4 October 2026 the public Asset Hunter site reported commit 149836b4 as its build, and that commit was the head of its public main branch at the same moment. The two facts were read from the site and the repository rather than inferred from a deploy message, and a reader can repeat the check.

That is a stronger claim than any other project on this site can currently support. It establishes which source produced the page in front of you. It does not establish that the catalogue is complete, that any individual entry has cleared rights, or that the same commit will be live tomorrow. One observation of one origin on one day is what it is.
What a private readout cannot

The other eight projects are described from a shareable readout. Their states are accurate to the best of a dated human review, and this site will not pretend otherwise: the dossier for each one carries its own review date, its own source description and the boundary its state does not cross.

The asymmetry is worth stating plainly rather than smoothing over. A public repository lets a reader audit the record; a private one asks them to trust the operator. Both are legitimate records. Presenting the second as though it were the first would be the exact overstatement this publication exists to avoid.

content.quote: A dated summary is evidence about a person. A pinned commit is evidence about a build.

children.text: The work still open

Asset Hunter was public and moving on the review date, with 34 possibilities in the published catalogue and 53 issues plus one image-optimisation pull request open. The open work that matters is not feature count. It is rights correction and takedown, security and hostile-content review of a public catalogue, and production release evidence with a restore drill.
Until those exist, the catalogue is a growing public reference rather than a dependable one. Its dossier says so, and names those three as the next proofs.

data.title: Four projects solved four different problems.
data.deck: A portfolio review proposed extracting one shared agent-and-browser safety layer from the games and this site. Reading the actual implementations says the opposite: these are four specific failures with four earned answers, and a shared layer would have had to pick a side in each.
data.source_reference: A portfolio analysis supplied for this review date, checked against the private repositories and the deployed origins of Bubbles, SHOALSHOT, Fighter, Asset Hunter and Woodhouse on 5 October 2026. The recommendation is recorded because it was tested and did not survive; no private issue, pull request or conversation body is reproduced.
data.lead: The strongest claim in the review was that several projects had independently reinvented the same machinery and should stop. Reading the implementations, they had not reinvented anything. They had each hit a different failure.
data.lesson: Repetition of vocabulary is not repetition of semantics. Before extracting what looks like a shared layer, check whether the failures are the same failure.

children.text: The claim, stated fairly

A portfolio analysis of this factory concluded that the clearest hidden asset was not any individual game but the autonomous-engineering machinery the games kept rebuilding: agent contracts, browser contention, deterministic evidence, deployment verification, long-run reporting. It called that repetition the strongest signal in the factory, and recommended a narrowly scoped spike to extract the smallest shared layer and make three projects consume it.

That is a reasonable reading of a portfolio described from the outside. Four projects all run agents against browsers. Four projects all capture screenshots and gate on them. Four projects all verify deployments. The surface really does look like one capability wearing four uniforms.
What the implementations actually do
The proposal came with its own condition attached: verify first, and if the semantics are not the same, do not manufacture the abstraction. So we read them. Four capabilities, four different answers.

Browser contention. Bubbles inspects the process table, walks process ancestry, and refuses to start when another test lane is running — and it separates a person's interactive browser from an automation lane, because those are different claims about the host. SHOALSHOT takes a different shape entirely: an atomic lockfile with liveness reaping and a bounded wait, guarding a resource it owns. Same symptom, different blast radius, different mechanism, different failure mode if you get it wrong. Fighter does neither; it lets the operating system pick a port.

Visual evidence. Bubbles compares against checked-in images with a pixel-difference tolerance, because some of its frames are genuinely animated and a strict comparison would be permanently red. SHOALSHOT compares byte-for-byte, because it pins the clock and the locale and can therefore demand exactness. These are opposite engineering choices about what a passing comparison means. Bubbles risks letting a real change through; SHOALSHOT risks a false alarm. A shared helper would have had to choose, and each project chose against the other's failure.

Long-run reporting. Three projects, three different ideas of what an agent's report is allowed to rest on: an executable terminal proof checked against live repository state, a version-controlled ledger with claims and worktree health, and a written execution contract with a dated backlog census that openly admits its default-branch rules are procedural rather than enforced.

Deployment verification. Four mechanisms, no shared shape. This site publishes a named identity schema and fails a deploy that does not report the fingerprint it intended to ship. Asset Hunter carries its own commit in page metadata, answers a version endpoint, and ships a freshness gate that once wrongly declared a site stale seconds after it deployed. Fighter and SHOALSHOT each wrote their own release manifests. The one artefact genuinely shared across the factory is a doctrine document, referenced by name from more than one repository.
What survived
Two things, and neither is a framework.

The first is a pattern rather than a library: the projects learned the same lessons in the same order and recorded them. One project found that a screenshot tool's update mode rewrote only the baseline that had actually changed and reported everything green — and the fix for that became doctrine in another repository, cited by name. Cross-project learning happened in the reasoning, deliberately, with no code moving between repositories.

In the safety and release mechanisms inspected on 5 October 2026, no shared code dependency was found. Each mechanism answered a different failure. This dated finding does not rule out reuse in another subsystem; the 10 October music capability review records LoftwahFM separately.

content.quote: The shared asset is the argument, not the module.

children.text: What this site does with it

Nothing is being extracted. The honest outcome of the check is the outcome the recommendation allowed for: no shared primitive, and no justification for one. Manufacturing a framework here would have been the exact failure this publication exists to catch — an abstraction justified by the existence of complicated code rather than by a shared failure.

There is one concrete gap worth naming, and it is not about a shared layer. This site publishes a build-identity shape and describes it as intended for reuse across the factory. No other project in the factory has adopted it; each wrote its own. A published protocol with no adopters is a claim about intent, not about the fleet, and it should be described that way until something else actually uses it.
The part that was worth the exercise

The useful outcome is not an artefact. It is that a portfolio-level claim about this factory turned out to be checkable, and got checked. A recommendation arrived with a verification condition attached; the condition was honoured; the recommendation lost.

That is the whole method in one pass. A supplied analysis is a hypothesis with good reasoning behind it, not a fact to be republished. Where it matched the evidence we adopted it — including its most uncomfortable finding, which is that Asset Hunter's own backup drill reports that nobody has used it yet. Where it did not match, we recorded the disagreement rather than smoothing it over.

data.title: The empty tables are the answer.
data.deck: Asset Hunter's backup drill found that the tables holding a stranger's rating, rights report or dispute have never had a row. The useful part is not the zero. It is that the product found the zero, wrote it down, and refused to call the drill a pass.
data.source_reference: The public Asset Hunter repository and its production backup manifest, reviewed 5 October 2026. Counts are read from the project's own recorded backup; nothing is estimated.
data.lead: A catalogue grew to forty possibilities and learned to name the exact commit it was built from. In the same week, a backup recorded that nobody has rated it, reported it, disputed it, or asked for anything to be left uncrawled.
data.lesson: A negative measurement taken and published is worth more than a positive one inferred. The tables that would hold a user's judgement are empty, and the product says so in its own words rather than shipping around it.

children.text: What the backup says

The production backup taken on 4 October 2026 lists the tables it captured and how many rows each held. The administrator account and its passkey were there, one row each. The schema was there. Eighty-seven revisions were there. The catalogue was there, with forty examples and four curated collections.

The tables that exist so that somebody other than the author can act were empty. Ratings: zero. Rights reports: zero. Disputes: zero. Requests to exclude a source: zero. Moderation audit events: zero.
Why that is the most valuable thing in the project

This is the distinction the whole factory keeps trying to make, appearing for once as a number rather than as a principle. Building a discovery engine is implementation. Shipping it is release. Publishing the commit it was built from is production verification. None of those is demand.

Demand is a person rating something they found, reporting a rights problem they recognised, or disputing a judgement the catalogue made about them. Every mechanism for that exists and works. Not one person has used any of them.

A portfolio review supplied this week reached the same conclusion from the outside and called Asset Hunter the strongest standalone product candidate. Both readings are worth keeping. The product is the most complete thing in the factory. On demonstrated external use it is at zero, and it is the only project that can say so precisely.

content.quote: An empty table restoring as an empty table is not evidence that a row in it ever will.
content.attribution: Asset Hunter restore drill, reviewed 5 October 2026

children.text: The gate that refused to pass

The obvious response to a drill that finds empty tables is to make the drill green. This one does the opposite: it exits non-zero over exactly that condition, and says in its own documentation that a drill reporting green across untested tables is the failure it exists to prevent.

That is the behaviour worth copying. A verification step that cannot fail is decoration. This one can fail, it fails loudly for an honest reason, and the failure is about the state of the world rather than about the health of the code.
What an empty table does not say

It does not say nobody has read the site. Reading is not recorded. It does not say the catalogue is wrong, or that anyone arrived and found nothing, or that anyone arrived, was served, and left without a reason that produces a row.

It says precisely this: no one has rated, reported, disputed or requested exclusion. Recorded behaviour is not the world, and this record should not be read as a verdict on the product. It is a measurement, taken honestly, of the thing this factory currently has no evidence for.
What would change it is cheap and unglamorous: outside builders and agents doing real hunts, and then saying what they used. That is the next proof. Another mechanism is not.

data.deck: Protocol 11 leads a new review of nine projects. The useful progress is in the game itself: a Journey, recovery, sound and art, backed by a reported production release. Elsewhere, a healthy live build can still be ahead of—or behind—the source.

children.text: Protocol 11 takes the lead

The House Circuit now gives the game a twelve-stage Journey with distinct mastery conditions and safe progress migration. Solo GO NUCLEAR has undo and restart, including the ability to roll back a bot reply. Room and cast artwork, stable theme geometry and refreshed sound make those systems feel part of the same game.

The supplied report records a settled production release matching the reviewed source, deployed asset hashes, readiness checks and live Chromium and WebKit gameplay checks. That is reported production verification, not a claim that Woodhouse has repeated the qualification. Physical iPhone play, sustained sessions and final art judgement still need their own evidence.
A strong release can sit behind newer source

SHOALSHOT is the clearest example. Its proven production build is healthy. Later first-catch Field Note work exposed recovery and browser failures, and the newer source stayed unreleased. Holding production at the qualified version is useful release discipline. The remaining question is also a design question: should automatic fire interrupt the player with a blocking discovery reveal?

Bubbles and Asset Hunter have newer source than the latest exact production receipt in the supplied report. Bubbles is resolving interaction and evidence debt. Asset Hunter has broadened from GitHub discovery to source-neutral ingestion, with a local folder, byte inspection and portable packs. Those are real implementation gains. They still need current release proof and outside use.
The rest of the portfolio has different work ahead

Fighter is turning observed battle failures into presentation changes and useful gates. LoftwahFM has a capable listener but a paused delivery lane. Pirates still needs source parity before expansion. MAX cannot turn software qualification into evidence that someone can find a real walker. Club needs renewed execution of its hospitality journey.

Each dossier now carries the 7 October report review, its source and the next proof. The older snapshots remain readable. Reviewing a supplied report is distinct from independently inspecting every repository or every live deployment.
Better judgement is the factory improvement

Across the report, the most encouraging behaviour is agents playing the products and finding defects that a ticket did not predict. A skipped ending, an unreachable catch, a battle that measures well but reads badly: the integrated experience supplies the requirement.

The response should stay small and concrete. Keep the always-on instructions short. Load detailed guidance when the work needs it. Adopt a tool at a real seam, give every process addition a failure it prevents, and retire a check when its original requirement no longer exists.

Model choice belongs to this dated account of the work. GPT 6.1 Sol is what the operator reports using for the recent Protocol 11 work; it is not a permanent rule for the factory. The durable rule is to put capable judgement at the point where it changes the outcome.

children.text: What changes the next decision

An agent can follow the upstream contract and its own game issue, select a compatible client, then record the installed version, deployment and listening evidence. New consumers enter through reviewed project identities and a capability review; no fixed five-game registry determines who may join.

Technical intelligence is useful when it changes a concrete compatibility or quality decision. Product intelligence is useful when it identifies an audience and a cheap demand test. Supplied reports remain hypotheses until checked against sources; a plausible pitch does not establish demand. Those investigations belong in their existing work, rather than another generator or recurring orchestration service.

children.text: Give people a reason to keep listening.

Dead Air Department and Smoko Circuit are published curated shows. Their technical release is distinct from a repeatable autonomous production operation and from human judgement of acting, comedy and pacing. Topical satire, evergreen material and recurring characters should coexist, with correction, expiry, provenance, spending and fallback handled by the owning programme.
The next useful evidence is material people choose to hear again. Producing more audio, adding another provider or collecting playback events does not by itself establish entertainment value.
A playable game still has to feel good.

Protocol 11’s progress is substantial, including its playable Journey and native radio. Current player reports still identify automatic hand reordering and shifting targets, unclear layoff destinations, insufficient Flaming feedback and desktop scrolling that hides laid-down groups. Interaction should support a predictable consecutive play, clear legal destinations and stable geometry on desktop and phone. Inspecting those root behaviours matters more than preserving an immature implementation or adding another cosmetic highlight.

Woodhouse now represents the shared radio relationship using the existing dossiers, dated statuses, capability review and evidence. Historical reviews remain dated, and unrelated projects are not given a fresh delivery claim. The same records serve readers and agent facts.

The useful next moves sit with their existing owners: Protocol 11 interaction correctness; FM soundtrack publishing, station mixing and entertaining programming; then discoverable installation, persuasive artwork and satisfying rewards. Reuse should make each product stronger while preserving independent identity, offline behaviour and release gates.

data.title: The tests passed. The game still looked wrong.
data.initial_belief: Responsive geometry and screenshot checks were sufficient to prevent major UI quality failures.
data.what_happened: The interface passed automated checks while remaining compositionally poor.
data.evidence: Geometry checks confirmed containment and expected bounds; they did not establish hierarchy or product quality.
data.root_cause: The system measured containment and geometry, not visual hierarchy or product judgement.
data.factory_change: Visual review of the whole experience, complete journeys and copy became distinct review stages.
data.later_reuse: The same distinction later informed visual review of Bubbles, as described in the public dispatch.
